notes.meaning: God gave this message to Jeremiah in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, which was also the first year of Nebuchadnezzar's rule in Babylon. This was a major turning point in history when Babylon defeated Egypt and became the dominant world power. God made sure His people knew that the rising world empire was part of His sovereign plan.

Jeremiah addressed the entire population of Judah and all the residents living in Jerusalem. Because this word came directly from the Lord, every citizen was accountable to hear and obey it. The prophet spoke openly so that no one in the nation could claim they were left without warning.

Jeremiah reminded the people that he had faithfully preached God's word to them for twenty-three years. He had begun during the thirteenth year of godly King Josiah and had worked tirelessly, yet the people constantly refused to listen. Their long history of stubbornness showed that their hearts were deeply hardened against the Lord.

The Lord had not relied on Jeremiah alone, but had repeatedly sent many other prophets to give the same warning. These messengers worked with great urgency, rising early and striving to turn the people back to God. Still, the people closed their ears and refused to pay attention.

Every prophet brought the same simple message: turn away from evil deeds and stop worshipping handmade idols. If the people would truly repent, God promised they could stay peacefully in the land He had given their ancestors forever. God took no pleasure in punishing them and promised to do them no harm if they remained faithful to Him.

Judah deliberately chose not to listen to the Lord's warnings. By clinging to false idols made with their own hands, they provoked God's righteous anger. In the end, their stubborn rebellion brought terrible ruin upon themselves, not upon God.

Because Judah refused to hear God's messengers of mercy, the Lord announced He would summon the armies of the north. He referred to Nebuchadnezzar as His servant because the Babylonian king was an instrument carrying out God's divine justice. Babylon and its allies would sweep over Judah and its neighbours, leaving the land in complete, horrifying ruins.

God warned that all normal, joyful daily life would be wiped out across the land. The sounds of wedding celebrations and music would fall silent. Even the daily grinding of grain for bread and the comforting glow of household lamps would disappear entirely.

The whole country of Judah would become an empty wasteland, and the surviving people would serve Babylon for seventy years. This fixed period punished the nation for centuries of neglecting God's laws, including the Sabbath rests for the land. At the same time, giving a set number of years offered comfort to faithful believers that their exile would eventually end.

differ.view: The seventy years are an exact chronological period running from the first taking of Jerusalem in 606 BC to the decree of Cyrus.
The seventy years should be understood as a round number representing a full lifetime of captivity.

notes.meaning: When the seventy years ended, God promised to hold Babylon and its king fully accountable for their wickedness and pride. Even though God had used Babylon to discipline His people, the Babylonians acted out of cruel, selfish motives and deserved punishment. Babylon would then fall and be reduced to lasting ruins.

differ.view: Because ancient Babylon was not permanently destroyed in a single day, this prophecy points forward to a rebuilt city of Babylon that will be destroyed during the end times.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Verses 12 to 14 were added by a later editor who adapted the promise of the seventy years from Jeremiah 29:10.

notes.meaning: Every judgment that Jeremiah wrote down against Babylon and other nations would be carried out to the letter. God's spoken word always accomplishes what He promises, proving that Jeremiah was a true prophet. The warnings in this book were certain because the Lord Himself stands behind them.

The mighty Babylonians who had made slaves of other nations would themselves be conquered and enslaved. Powerful kings and great nations, led by the Medes and Persians, would conquer Babylon. God promised to repay the oppressors precisely according to the cruelty they had shown to others.

God gave Jeremiah a prophetic vision in which the prophet received a cup filled with the wine of God's holy wrath. Jeremiah was commanded to hand this cup to the nations, picturing the terrible judgment coming upon them. When people drank it, they would stagger and lose their minds under the horrifying shock of war.

Jeremiah obeyed the Lord by taking the cup and delivering God's judgment to all the nations he was told to address. He did not physically travel to every country, but he faithfully announced God's decrees from Jerusalem. His obedience showed that God has authority over every ruler and country on earth.

Judgment began with God's own house, starting at Jerusalem, the towns of Judah, and their royal leaders. Because they possessed God's law and temple, their guilt was greater when they rebelled. They would be left in ruins, becoming an object of shocking horror and a curse to all who saw them.

The cup of wrath was next handed to Pharaoh of Egypt, along with his officials and people, because Judah had falsely trusted in Egypt for military help. The judgment then reached foreign groups living in Egypt, the ruler of Uz, and the Philistine cities of Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and what was left of Ashdod. None of these pagan powers could escape God's reach.

Next on the list were Edom, Moab, and Ammon, neighbouring kingdoms related to Israel by blood. God's judgment then turned west to the wealthy Phoenician trading cities of Tyre and Sidon, as well as the coastlands across the sea. Human wealth, strong island fortresses, and sea trade could not protect them from the coming invasion.

God directed His warnings to the nomadic desert tribes of Dedan, Tema, and Buz, who lived in the remote corners of the wilderness. The kings of Arabia, the desert wanderers, and the rulers of Zimri, Elam, and Media were also summoned to drink the cup. No tribe or nation was too distant or isolated for God's justice to find them.

The judgment was decreed against all the northern kingdoms, whether near or far, covering every realm on earth. Finally, after all other nations drank, the king of Sheshach would drink the cup too. Sheshach was a code name for Babylon, showing that the great conqueror would ultimately face the very same ruin it had brought on others.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The clause mentioning the king of Sheshach was not part of the original prophecy, but was inserted later by a copyist or editor.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah was told to command the nations to drink deeply until they vomited, collapsed, and could not get up again because of the invading sword. If any kingdom proudly refused to accept this sentence, the prophet had to tell them they had no choice. No human army or stubborn will can turn away the decreed judgments of the Almighty.

The Lord pointed out that He was already bringing destruction on Jerusalem, the city that bore His own name. If God did not spare His chosen people when they sinned, pagan nations could never expect to go unpunished. The sword of God's holy justice would sweep across all the inhabitants of the earth without exception.

differ.view: These global declarations point beyond the ancient Babylonian invasion to the worldwide judgments of the future Great Tribulation.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah was told to declare that the Lord would roar from heaven like a lion attacking its prey. His mighty voice would shout against His own land and against all the people of the world. Just as workers tread grapes in a winepress with loud shouts, God would execute His holy judgment on human wickedness.

The sound of judgment would echo to the ends of the earth as God brought a formal legal charge against all nations. He enters into a courtroom dispute with the human race, showing that His anger is entirely fair and lawful. In the end, the unrepentant wicked will be handed over to the destroying sword.

Disaster would spread from one nation to another like an unstoppable hurricane rolling in from the far reaches of the earth. Those struck down by the Lord would lie dead across the land in numbers so great that no one would be left to mourn or bury them. Their bodies would simply lie exposed on the open ground like refuse.

The kings and political rulers, described here as shepherds and leaders of the flock, are told to howl and roll in ashes in bitter sorrow. The day had arrived for their slaughter and scattering, and they would crash to pieces like a fine piece of delicate pottery. When disaster struck, even the strongest and most privileged leaders would find no way to escape.

Loud wailing rises from these ruined rulers because the Lord has completely destroyed the land and people they once governed. Even places that had long lived in calm peace and security were wiped out under God's burning anger. Earthly stability cannot survive when God brings a nation to account for its sins.

The Lord has left His dwelling place like a fierce lion coming out of its lair to hunt down its prey. Without His divine protection, the land was left completely desolate before the cruel sword of the Babylonian conqueror. This destruction came not by chance, but as the direct outcome of the Lord's righteous anger.
